passage: The case for monitoring employees at work usually rests on two claims. The first is that the employer is paying for the worker's time and is therefore entitled to know how that time is spent. The second is that the worker has agreed to the arrangement: the monitoring policy was set out in the contract, and nobody was forced to sign it. Both claims sound reasonable, and both, I think, prove much less than their defenders suppose.

Take the argument from payment first. An employer buys a worker's labour, not the worker; the wage secures a certain kind of effort over a certain period, and it has never been understood to include a right to observe everything a person does while that effort is being given. A firm that pays a carpenter by the day may inspect the cabinets she builds, but it does not thereby acquire a claim to read her letters during lunch. The argument from consent fares little better. Agreement given by someone who needs the job, in a market where most comparable employers impose similar terms, tells us that the terms were accepted, not that they were fair. Consent of this kind can settle a dispute about what was agreed; it cannot settle whether the agreement should have been offered.

The deeper difficulty is what continuous monitoring does to work itself. When every keystroke and pause is recorded, the employee learns to perform for the record rather than for the task. A support worker whose calls are timed will cut short a conversation with a confused customer even when a longer one would solve the problem; an office worker whose idle minutes are logged will keep the screen busy instead of stopping to think. The record begins to replace the judgement it was supposed to check, and the trust on which most skilled work depends, the expectation that a person will use discretion well when no one is looking, quietly erodes. There is an irony here as well: the information that monitoring yields grows less useful the more thoroughly it is collected, because what it captures is increasingly a display staged for the watcher.

None of this means that employers may never watch. Where a job carries a specific and serious risk, such as handling cash, operating dangerous machinery or opening confidential records, targeted checks are a reasonable response to that risk, and most employees understand them as such. The test I would propose is therefore not whether monitoring was agreed to, but whether it is tied to an identifiable hazard and limited to what that hazard requires. General surveillance, justified only by the employer's wish to know, fails that test, however clearly it has been written into the contract.

passage: As tariffs have fallen over the past several decades, attention in trade disputes has shifted to a less visible kind of obstacle: the technical standards a product must meet before it can be sold. Rules on labelling, safety testing, permitted additives and packaging are written for reasons that sound unimpeachable, and many of them are exactly what they claim to be. But a rule can protect consumers and domestic producers at the same time, and it is not always easy to say which purpose is doing the work.

The usual complaint is that standards are protectionism by other means, and examples are easy to imagine. Suppose a country requires that cheese be aged in wooden barrels of a particular kind, a method its own dairies have used for generations, while foreign producers age theirs in steel vessels that yield a product no less safe. The rule says nothing explicit about origin, and its authors need never mention foreign cheese at all, yet its effect is almost that of a ban on imports. A tariff of this severity would be denounced at once; dressed as a quality rule, it may pass unnoticed for years.

It does not follow, however, that every standard which burdens importers is suspect. Almost any rule imposes costs on foreign firms, if only because they must learn it, and societies differ honestly in the risks they will tolerate. One country may accept a pesticide residue that another refuses, not because its farmers lobbied but because its citizens weigh the balance between price and caution differently. To treat all such divergence as disguised protection would be to deny countries the right to set their own levels of acceptable risk, which is a large part of what self-government means.

The more useful test is therefore not whether a standard falls harder on foreigners, but whether its burden is necessary to the purpose it states. A rule that specifies an outcome, such as a maximum level of bacteria, leaves producers free to reach it by any method and so admits anyone who can meet it. A rule that specifies a method, when other methods would achieve the same outcome, deserves closer scrutiny, because the extra cost it imposes buys no additional safety. The distinction will not settle every dispute; outcomes can be hard to measure, and a method is sometimes prescribed precisely because checking the outcome is impractical. But it shifts the argument from motives, which are hard to prove, to fit, which can at least be examined.

passage: A familiar way of thinking about Western art music divides the creative labour with reassuring neatness. The composer makes the work and records it in a score; the performer's task is to realise the score faithfully, adding as little of himself as the music allows. On this view the score is the work, or at least its complete specification, and a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains. Its attractions are considerable. It accounts for our confidence that two strikingly different performances are nevertheless performances of the same composition, and it furnishes the critic with a standard: the performer who alters the notes has made a mistake, whatever the result sounds like.

The difficulty is that notation specifies far less than the view requires. A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less, but a great deal of what listeners hear as the character of a performance is left open or indicated only roughly. A marking that asks for a loud passage does not say how loud, and the right loudness in a small room is not the right loudness in a large hall. A word indicating a lively tempo admits a range of speeds wide enough to make one performance sound urgent and another relaxed. Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase, or how to weigh the notes of a chord against one another. These are not trivial details that a faithful performer can safely settle at random; they are much of what makes the music sound the way it does.

One response is to swing to the opposite extreme and say that the work simply is the performance, the score being no more than a set of instructions that each performer completes as she pleases. This rescues the performer's creative contribution, but at a considerable theoretical price. It cannot explain why some performances strike informed listeners as wrong-headed even when every note is in place, or why a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed has done something worse than make an unusual choice. If the score were merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements, and yet musicians make them constantly and with considerable agreement.

That agreement points to what both positions conspicuously omit. Scores are never interpreted in isolation. They are read by musicians trained in a practice: a shared and largely unwritten understanding of what the marks mean in a given style, which conventions apply, what kinds of freedom are expected and where those freedoms stop. In music of one period a trill is understood to begin on the note above; in another it begins on the main note; the score is usually silent on the point, and the practice supplies the answer. The work, on this account, is neither the marks alone nor whatever a given performance makes of them, but the marks as a practice reads them. Fidelity is owed to that combination.

It may be objected that practices evolve, so that the work would apparently evolve with them, which seems absurd. But the objection establishes considerably less than it appears to. Practices do change, slowly, and the identity of a work is correspondingly less fixed than the first view supposed; that is a cost worth accepting, since it matches how musicians actually argue about performances. What does not follow is that anything goes. A practice at any moment draws lines that its members can defend, and a performer who knowingly crosses them is making a claim that must be argued for, not exercising a right.

passage: The familiar explanation of teenage recklessness is ignorance: adolescents take risks because they do not understand the dangers, or because they believe, in some half-formed way, that harm happens only to other people. If that were the whole story, the remedy would be straightforward. Teach young people the facts about speeding, drugs and unprotected sex, and their behaviour should improve. Schools and governments have spent heavily on precisely this remedy, and its results have often been modest.

One reason is that the premise is weaker than it looks. When adolescents are asked, in a calm setting, to estimate the dangers of various activities, their answers are often not very different from those of adults, and by the middle teens many reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do. What distinguishes them is less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations. Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature; decisions taken in the company of friends, under excitement, look very different. In laboratory games that reward bold choices, adolescents have been found to take noticeably more chances when they know their friends are watching, while the presence of an audience makes much less difference to adults.

A plausible account of this pattern appeals to the uneven timing of development. The systems that make rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense appear to become more responsive around puberty, while the capacities for restraint and planning continue to mature into the early twenties. For several years, then, the accelerator is more sensitive than the brake, and the gap shows most clearly when peers raise the value of a daring act. It should be said that accounts of this kind are easily overstated. Brains do not determine behaviour on their own, adolescents differ widely, and plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care.

If the account is broadly right, it has an uncomfortable implication for policy: the most effective interventions may be those that change the situations adolescents find themselves in rather than the beliefs they carry into them. Rules that limit the number of young passengers a new driver may carry, or arrangements that make the safe choice the socially easy one, work with the grain of adolescent decision-making rather than against it. The account also suggests a more generous reading of adolescence itself. A heightened sensitivity to peers is not simply a defect awaiting repair; it is part of what drives young people to leave the family, form their own alliances and try what their elders would not. The same disposition that makes a reckless dare attractive makes new friendships and new ideas attractive too.

passage: The model of the national park that spread across much of the world in the twentieth century rested on a simple picture: nature is most fully itself where people are absent, and the task of conservation is to keep them out. Boundaries were drawn, guards were posted, and in many places the people who had lived within the new boundaries, herding, gathering, farming small plots or hunting, were moved elsewhere. Critics have come to call this approach fortress conservation, and the name captures both its method and its mood.

The picture of untouched nature was often historically false. Many landscapes that visitors admired as wilderness had been shaped for centuries by the people who were then removed: grasslands kept open by grazing and deliberate burning, forests whose composition reflected generations of selective harvesting and planting. Removing those people did not return the land to an original state; it began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline. The costs to the displaced were, of course, more direct: the loss of homes, of access to food and medicine, of graves and sacred places, often with little or no compensation.

It would be too simple, however, to conclude that local residents are always the best stewards and that exclusion is never justified. Communities change, markets reach into forests, and a population that once harvested lightly may, under new pressures, begin to clear or hunt at rates the land cannot sustain. Some species, particularly those that are very sensitive to disturbance, may genuinely need areas where human presence is kept to a minimum. The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading as the image of untouched wilderness that it seeks to replace.

What the critique of fortress conservation establishes, then, is not a rule but a burden of proof. Exclusion imposes certain and heavy costs on identifiable people, while its benefits to wildlife are often assumed rather than shown. Where those who would be displaced have a long record of use compatible with the values being protected, the presumption should lie with their remaining, and with arrangements that give them a real share in managing the land. Where that record is absent, or where a species' needs are demonstrably incompatible with human use, exclusion may be defended; but it must be defended, case by case, rather than taken as the natural form of protection.

passage: For much of the modern period the doctrine of sovereignty was understood as a wall. Within its borders a state was answerable to no outside authority, and what it did to its own population, however terrible, was a matter of domestic jurisdiction. The rule had a defensible rationale. A world in which any power could enter another's territory whenever it disapproved of how that territory was governed would be a world of permanent intervention, in which the strong would always find reasons to correct the weak. Non-interference was less a tribute to the virtue of governments than a device for keeping their quarrels within bounds.

The atrocities of the late twentieth century made the wall look like a shield for murderers, and a new formula emerged to reconcile the old principle with the demand to act. Sovereignty, it was argued, is not a privilege but a responsibility: a state holds it on condition that it protects its people, and a state that massacres them, or cannot stop others from doing so, forfeits its claim to be left alone. The formula is elegant, because it seems to dissolve the conflict rather than adjudicate it. Intervention to stop mass killing no longer violates sovereignty, since the sovereignty in question has already been forfeited.

The elegance is partly an illusion. The formula does not remove the hard question but relocates it. Someone must still decide when a government has failed badly enough to forfeit its rights, and in practice that someone is usually the state or coalition proposing to intervene, which is to say a party with interests of its own in the outcome. The old doctrine at least gave a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody. The new one replaces that answer with a judgement, and judgements made by the powerful about the weak have a history that should make anyone cautious. It is not a cynical point that intervention has tended to occur where the interveners had strategic reasons to be and not elsewhere; it is an observation about how a discretionary rule will be used.

None of this is an argument for returning to the wall. A principle that obliged the world to watch a massacre it could stop would purchase order at a price few would accept once they had seen what it meant. The question is not whether sovereignty may ever yield, but how the decision that it should yield is to be made credible. Here the procedure matters as much as the facts. An intervention authorised by a broad body of states, through rules that apply to friends as well as to enemies, carries a legitimacy that one undertaken by a single power on its own assessment cannot, even when the atrocities alleged are equally real.

The difficulty is that procedure can fail in the other direction. The bodies most able to confer legitimacy are also those in which a single interested member can block action, and the insistence on proper authorisation can become a reason for doing nothing while the killing continues. There is no formula that escapes this. A world that refuses all unauthorised intervention will sometimes stand by when it should act, and a world that permits it will sometimes see intervention used as a pretext. The honest position is to admit that we are choosing which of these failures to risk, and to stop pretending that a change of vocabulary has spared us the choice.

passage: Statements of chance are among the most familiar in science and ordinary life, and among the hardest to interpret. When we say that a fair coin has a chance of one half of landing heads, what are we saying? The most influential answer identifies chance with frequency: the chance of heads is the proportion of heads in a long run of tosses, or the limit towards which that proportion tends as the run is extended without end. The answer has the great merit of tying chance to something that can be counted, and it explains why observed frequencies are our main evidence about chances.

Its difficulties begin with the single case. A particular coin may be tossed once and then melted down; a particular patient either will or will not recover from a particular operation. Yet we speak readily of the chance that this toss lands heads or that this patient recovers, and such judgements guide real decisions. The frequency view can treat them only by placing the single case in a class of similar cases and borrowing the frequency of the class. And here a second difficulty appears, because every case belongs to many classes. The patient is a man of sixty, a non-smoker, a resident of a particular city, someone treated by a particular surgeon, and the recovery rates in these classes may differ considerably. Which frequency is the patient's chance?

Dissatisfaction with this reference class problem has led many to prefer a propensity view, on which chance is a physical tendency of a particular set-up to produce a given outcome, a property the single toss or the single operation possesses whether or not any long run ever occurs. The propensity view handles the single case gracefully, but at a price. It is unclear what a propensity is, beyond a name for whatever it is that frequencies are evidence of, and the view does not escape the problem it was meant to solve. The tendency of a set-up depends on how the set-up is described: the toss described as a toss of a fair coin has one propensity, while the toss described down to the exact force and angle of the flick may have another, close to certainty.

The persistence of the problem across both views suggests that it is not a defect peculiar to either but a feature of chance itself. A chance is not a property an event has simply, but a property it has relative to a specification of the circumstances. Asking for the chance of an event, full stop, is like asking for the speed of a train without saying relative to what: the question is not unanswerable but incomplete. What remains open, and must be settled by our purposes rather than by the world, is which specification to use. For a gambler who cannot measure the flick, the description 'fair coin' is the relevant one; for a physicist with a high-speed camera, it is not.

Some will feel that this concedes too much, making chance a matter of perspective rather than a feature of the world. But relativity to a description is not the same as subjectivity. Once the specification is fixed, the chance is fixed too, and two observers who adopt the same description and disagree about the chance cannot both be right. Velocity is no less objective for being relative to a frame. What the account gives up is only the idea that there is a single privileged description, the one nature itself would choose, and it is far from clear that anything in science requires such a description.

passage: Few political ideals are invoked as often, or defined as loosely, as the rule of law. In one usage it names a set of formal properties of a legal order: laws should be general rather than aimed at particular persons, public rather than secret, prospective rather than retroactive, clear enough to be followed, stable enough to be relied on, and applied by courts that are independent of those who hold power. In another usage the phrase stands for a much larger package. A state governed by the rule of law, on this richer view, is one that also protects fundamental rights, holds free elections and distributes its burdens fairly. Whatever is admirable in a constitutional democracy tends to be gathered under the same heading.

The richer view has an obvious appeal. It seems perverse to praise a legal order for its clarity and consistency while it applies clear and consistent laws that strip a minority of its property or bar it from public life. Yet the inclusive definition carries a cost that its defenders seldom count. If the rule of law means everything good about a political system, the phrase ceases to pick out anything in particular. We lose the ability to say, of one regime, that its laws are cruel but at least public and predictable, or of another that it has excellent statutes on paper which officials ignore whenever it suits them. These are different failings, calling for different remedies, and a vocabulary that cannot separate them is a poorer instrument for judging governments, not a more generous one.

The formal conception, moreover, is not as morally empty as its critics allege. A law that is public and prospective allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to arrange their lives around it; a law applied by independent courts constrains the officials who administer it as well as the citizens who are subject to it. These are real goods even when the content of the law is objectionable, because they leave the governed some room to anticipate, avoid and contest what is done to them. It is also worth noticing that governments bent on oppression rarely find formal legality congenial. They tend to prefer secret directives, retroactive offences, vague charges that can be stretched to fit any critic, and enforcement that falls on enemies and spares friends. The formal requirements, in other words, get in the way of a great deal of injustice, even if they forbid none of it outright.

This last point should not be pressed too far. The tendency of formality to obstruct oppression is a matter of experience, not of logic, and experience includes regimes that pursued grave injustice through meticulously drafted, publicly promulgated and impartially enforced laws. A defender of the thin conception must concede that legality of this kind is compatible with deep wrong, and that its tendency to discourage abuse is a probability rather than a guarantee. What can be claimed is narrower: that formal legality is one distinct virtue a legal order may have or lack, that its absence makes most other wrongs easier to commit, and that we see it most clearly when we refuse to let it stand for every other virtue at once. Questions about whether the laws are just, whether the rulers were chosen freely and whether the burdens are fairly shared remain, on this view, as urgent as ever; they are simply different questions, and they deserve to be asked in their own terms.

passage: A familiar picture of the responsible thinker holds that she believes nothing on another's say-so until she has satisfied herself that the speaker is reliable. On this view, testimony is a second-class source of knowledge, legitimate only when it can be cashed out in the currency of one's own perception and reasoning: I may believe the timetable because I have found timetables accurate before, and I may believe my doctor because I have, or could obtain, evidence of her competence. The picture has the appeal of self-reliance. It seems to keep the knower in charge of what she knows.

The difficulty is that almost nobody could meet its demands, and the few who tried would know very little. Consider how much of what an ordinary adult believes was simply told to her: the shape of the continents, the date of her own birth, the existence of cells, the fact that a city she has never visited lies where the maps place it. To check the reliability of these sources she would have to rely on further sources, whose reliability would in turn need checking. The independent track record the picture asks for is itself largely assembled from testimony. A child who refused to believe her teachers until she had verified their credentials would never acquire the language in which credentials are described.

It does not follow that we may believe whatever we are told. The better view is that a hearer is entitled to accept what she is told unless she has some reason for doubt: a speaker with an evident motive to deceive, a claim that collides with what she already has good grounds to believe, a manner that suggests guesswork rather than knowledge. On this view the burden is reversed. Trust is the default, and it is suspicion, not acceptance, that must be earned by evidence. This is not credulity, because the default is sensitive to defeaters; the hearer who ignores a glaring sign of deceit is not exercising her entitlement but neglecting it.

Defenders of the stricter picture are right about one thing. A default of trust is only as good as the hearer's alertness to the signals that should override it, and that alertness is unevenly distributed and easily exploited. The con artist's whole craft consists in suppressing the cues that would trigger doubt. But this shows that we need to cultivate sensitivity to defeaters, not that we must abandon trust as a starting point. A community in which everyone demanded proof before belief would not be more rational than ours; it would merely be poorer in what it could collectively know.

passage: Until late in the twentieth century, many biologists expected that animals as different as a fly and a mouse would be built by largely different sets of genes. Their bodies seemed to have little in common: one has a hard external skeleton, six jointed legs and compound eyes, the other an internal skeleton, four limbs and eyes with a single lens. If form reflects the genes that make it, the reasoning went, such different forms must be made by different genes. What came instead was one of the great surprises of modern biology. A small kit of genes that direct development, deciding where the head goes, where limbs sprout and which segments become which, turned out to be shared, in recognisable versions, across almost the entire animal kingdom.

The most striking demonstrations concerned eyes. Eyes had long been thought to have evolved independently many times, so different are the eyes of insects, squid and vertebrates. Yet a gene needed for eye development in mice has a counterpart in flies, and when the mouse version is switched on in the wrong tissue of a developing fly, the fly grows extra eyes, fly eyes, on its legs or wings. The gene does not carry a blueprint of an eye. It acts more like a switch that says, in effect, 'build an eye here', leaving the details of construction to the many other genes that each lineage has in its own repertoire.

It is tempting to conclude that the evolution of form is mostly a matter of rewiring old switches rather than inventing new parts, and there is much truth in that. Changes in when and where toolkit genes are turned on can alter the number of segments, the length of a limb or the pattern on a wing without any change in the proteins the genes make. Because a single toolkit gene acts in many tissues, a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone. This helps explain why so much evolutionary change appears to lie in the regulatory regions of the genome.

Yet the shared toolkit should not be mistaken for a shared plan. That the same switch triggers eye-building in a fly and a mouse does not mean that their eyes are, in any useful sense, the same organ; the structures downstream of the switch were assembled separately, over hundreds of millions of years, from different materials. Common genes reveal a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled. The older view was wrong to assume that different forms require different genes; the newer enthusiasm risks the opposite error, of assuming that similar genes imply similar forms.

passage: In the design of a clinical trial, the placebo plays the role of nothing. Patients in one group receive the drug, patients in the other receive an inert imitation, and whatever improvement the second group shows is subtracted from the first as background noise. The logic is sound for its purpose, which is to establish whether a molecule does anything beyond the act of being given. But the habit of treating the placebo arm as a measure of nothing has encouraged a further and less defensible assumption, that the improvement seen there is not real, or at least not interesting.

It is both. What patients in a placebo group respond to is not the sugar in the pill but everything that surrounds it: the consultation, the explanation, the expectation of relief, the ritual of taking something at set hours, the attention of people whose job is to help. Some researchers prefer to speak of a 'meaning response' for this reason, since the inert pill is merely the occasion on which the meaning of being treated is delivered. On this view the placebo arm is not a blank but a measurement of how much the context of care can do by itself.

The standard objection to using such effects deliberately has been ethical. A placebo, it was assumed, works only if the patient is deceived, and deceiving patients violates the trust on which medicine depends. Several small trials have unsettled this assumption by giving patients pills that were openly described as inert and still recording improvements in symptoms that the patients reported themselves. The findings are preliminary, and it is not clear how much of the effect survives once the novelty of an unusual study wears off. Even so, they suggest that deception may be less essential to the response than was believed, and that the ritual may matter more than the belief that the pill is active.

Enthusiasts are quick to go further than the evidence allows. Responses to placebo are most consistent for symptoms that are experienced and reported, such as pain, nausea and fatigue; there is little reason to think that the meaning of a consultation can shrink a tumour or clear an infection. The more useful conclusion is not that doctors should prescribe sugar pills but that the manner of care is itself a part of treatment. A health system that shortens consultations to save money may be removing an active ingredient without ever recording the loss, because its effect was always filed under nothing.

passage: When a global fast-food chain enters a new country, the first thing commentators examine is its menu. If the chain serves the same burger it serves at home, critics see cultural flattening, the erosion of local tastes by a single corporate palate. If it introduces a spiced vegetable patty or a rice dish for the local market, its defenders announce that globalisation, far from erasing difference, accommodates it. Both sides agree, without ever saying so, that the menu is where the question of cultural influence will be settled.

That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. A menu is the part of a chain that is easiest to change and, for that very reason, the part that tells us least. What the chain actually exports is a format: a way of organising food, labour and time. The counter at which one orders without a waiter, the fixed price displayed in advance, the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month, the kitchen run like an assembly line by staff who can be trained in days: these travel intact, and they carry assumptions about efficiency and predictability that are far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient. A spiced patty served through such a system is a local flavour in a global grammar.

Yet it would be wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings wherever it goes, for customers bring meanings of their own. In some places a visit to a chain restaurant has been, at least for a time, a special occasion rather than a convenience: a clean, cool and respectable room in which a family can celebrate a birthday, or two young people can meet without attracting comment. The format was designed for speed, but the customers linger. They take a system built to minimise the time spent at the table and turn it into a place for spending time.

The interesting story, then, has three layers rather than one. The format is global and changes slowly; the meanings attached to it are local and can diverge sharply from what its designers intended; the menu sits between them, adjusted constantly in response to both. To read cultural influence from the menu alone is like judging the spread of a language by the loanwords it has picked up, while ignoring both its grammar and the uses to which its new speakers put it.

passage: When information was scarce, the economic problem it posed was one of supply: how to print, carry and store enough of it for the people who wanted it. That problem has largely been solved, and its solution has exposed another. The abundance of material has made scarce the one resource that every piece of it requires, namely the attention of those who are meant to receive it. Every article, message and video competes for the same limited hours of the same limited minds, and while the cost of producing one more piece of content has fallen almost to nothing, the supply of attention has not grown at all.

This shift explains a feature of modern commerce that once seemed puzzling, the enormous number of services offered at no charge. A search engine, a social network or a mobile game that costs its user nothing is not a gift; it is paid for with attention, which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers, so that the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded. Described in this way, the arrangement is not obviously unfair. Many people would gladly exchange a few seconds of distraction for a useful map or a convenient way of keeping in touch with distant friends, and for them the bargain may be a good one.

The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the fact that the price is never stated. When a product is sold for money, its price is a number that buyers can compare across sellers, and the comparison disciplines firms, since a shop that charges too much loses its customers to a cheaper rival. Attention has no such number attached to it. A user cannot easily tell whether one free application takes ten minutes of her day or two hours, still less whether a rival would take less, and so the competitive pressure that keeps money prices in check operates feebly, if at all. Firms competing for attention are therefore rewarded not for charging less of it but for extracting more, and the design of their products follows accordingly, towards endless feeds, automatic playback and notifications timed to recapture a wandering mind.

It does not follow that free services should be prohibited or that their users are dupes. What follows is narrower and, in a way, more practical: a market in which one side cannot see the price it pays will not protect that side as markets ordinarily do, and remedies should therefore aim at making the price visible. A service that reported to each user, plainly and regularly, how much time it had absorbed would not end the trade in attention, but it would give its users what every functioning market requires, a figure to compare.

passage: Few doctrines have been more often misunderstood by sympathetic outsiders than the Buddhist teaching of anatta, usually translated as 'no-self'. Stated baldly, as the claim that there is no self, it seems to invite an easy refutation: someone, after all, is entertaining the doctrine, and someone will be disappointed if it turns out to be false. Critics who press this point imagine that they have found a contradiction at the heart of the tradition. In fact they have mostly found a problem of translation, and behind it a mistaken assumption about what kind of claim the teaching was meant to be.

In the early discourses the teaching typically appears not as a thesis about what exists but as an exercise. The listener is led through the components that make up a person, which the tradition groups as bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, and is asked of each whether it is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it is under one's control. Since none of them passes these tests, none, the discourse concludes, should be regarded as 'mine', as what 'I am', or as 'my self'. The point of the exercise is practical. According to the tradition's own account of suffering, its origin lies in craving, and craving is sustained by the habit of treating changing and uncontrollable processes as possessions one must defend. To see that nothing in experience is fit to be owned in that way is to loosen the grip of the habit.

Read in this light, the easy refutation misses its target. The teaching does not deny that there is a stream of experiences, nor that the stream has a history, makes choices and bears their consequences; the same tradition has a great deal to say about all three. What it denies is that there is, in addition to the stream, an unchanging owner standing behind it, and it denies this chiefly because belief in such an owner is what makes us cling. A later dialogue makes the point with a chariot: the word names an assembly of axle, wheels and frame, and nothing is lost by admitting that there is no further chariot over and above the parts, arranged as they are. The person, likewise, is a convenient name for a functioning whole, not a hidden thing to which the whole belongs.

It would be too convenient, however, to conclude that the doctrine is purely therapeutic and therefore immune to philosophical scrutiny. A therapy that works by inducing a belief earns its authority only if the belief is warranted; otherwise it is a comforting fiction, and the tradition has never presented its teaching as a fiction. The exercise succeeds, by its own standards, because it reveals how things are. So the metaphysical question cannot be set aside; it can only be stated more precisely. The question is not whether anyone exists but whether a person is anything more than the organised stream, and on that question the doctrine takes a position that some philosophers in other traditions have also defended, and others have rejected, without anyone having settled the matter.

The lesson for the sympathetic outsider is therefore double. The easy refutation fails, because it attacks a claim the teaching does not make. But the easy defence fails too, because the teaching is not merely a technique; it is a technique whose authority rests on a claim about the self that may be true or false, and that deserves to be argued about on its merits rather than admired from a respectful distance.

passage: Labour law in most countries rests on a binary. A worker is either an employee, who accepts direction in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections, or an independent contractor, who sells a result, chooses her own methods and bears her own risks. The line was drawn for a world in which the difference was usually obvious: the clerk at a desk was one, the plumber who came to fix the office pipes was the other. Platform work has made the line hard to find. A driver who logs into an app chooses when to work and may refuse any job, which looks like independence; the same driver cannot set the fare, does not know which passenger comes next, and can be removed by an algorithm whose criteria she never sees, which looks very much like direction.

Two responses dominate the debate. One holds that platform workers are employees in all but name and that courts should simply say so. The other holds that flexibility is the whole attraction of such work, that many who do it also study or hold other jobs, and that imposing fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle would destroy the thing they value. Each side is right about what the other ignores. The first is right that the platform exercises a control over the terms of work that no genuine contractor would accept; the second is right that the employment bundle was designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer, and fits awkwardly onto someone who works eleven hours one week for three different apps and none the next.

What both share is the assumption that protections must come as a package attached to a status. That assumption is a historical accident rather than a principle. Some protections, such as a minimum rate for time actually worked, insurance against injury on the job or a right to be told why an account was suspended, depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible. Others, such as paid holidays calculated over a working year, are harder to translate, though not obviously impossible if entitlements accrue by the hour and follow the worker rather than the firm.

Unbundling has dangers of its own. A menu of separable protections invites firms to lobby for the cheapest selection, and a third category of worker, introduced to accommodate the platforms, could become a convenient place to move people who are at present employees. The case for unbundling is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed: forcing a new form of work into one of two old boxes guarantees that, whichever box is chosen, a large part of the reality will be misdescribed.

options.B: the package of fares, routes and passengers that a platform assigns to each driver who logs into its app.
options.C: the group of workers who share one employer and a fixed schedule, as clerks in an office traditionally did.
options.D: the set of protections and obligations that come together with the legal status of being an employee.

passage: A familiar lament holds that the public has broken into pieces. Where citizens once read the same few newspapers and watched the same evening bulletin, they now inhabit separate streams of information, each tuned to its audience's prior beliefs, and the common ground on which democratic argument depends is said to have eroded. The complaint is heard from commentators of every persuasion, each of whom tends to blame the media favoured by the other side. The lament contains a real worry, but it rests on a picture of the past that deserves scrutiny, and the remedies it suggests follow from the picture rather than from the worry.

The ideal of a single forum in which a whole society reasons together has an attractive genealogy. Its admirers point to the coffeehouses, reading societies and pamphlet wars of early modern Europe, where private individuals gathered to discuss public affairs as equals. Yet the gatherings so admired were open in principle and narrow in practice, confined largely to those with the leisure, literacy and standing to take part. The mass audiences of the broadcast era were broader, but their breadth was purchased by a different narrowing: millions listened, while very few were permitted to speak, and the range of views considered respectable was set by a small number of editors and producers. What looks in retrospect like common ground was in part a common silence about matters that the gatekeepers did not think worth raising.

None of this means the old arrangement had no merit. A shared stock of reported facts, however selectively assembled, gave opponents something definite to disagree about. Two people who had heard the same bulletin could argue over what to do about a strike or a drought without first arguing over whether it had happened. That is the genuine loss the lament points to, and it should not be dismissed. But it is worth being precise about what was lost. It was not chiefly that everyone attended to the same things, which was never a requirement of self-government and was always enforced partly by exclusion. It was that disputes about fact could be settled, or at least narrowed, by appeal to procedures and sources that people on both sides accepted.

Seen this way, the fragmentation of audiences matters less than the fragmentation of standards. Many publics can coexist in a healthy democracy, each attending to its own concerns, provided that when they collide they can appeal to shared ways of establishing what is true. A society in which different groups read different things but accept the same rules of evidence is plural, not broken. A society whose groups no longer recognise any common method for testing claims is in difficulty even if they all watch the same programme. The second condition is the more dangerous because it is harder to see: a shared screen can conceal the fact that its viewers no longer agree on what would count as showing that something is so.

The distinction has practical consequences. Nostalgia for the mass audience tends to recommend the impossible, the restoration of a few dominant outlets with the authority to define reality for everyone, and it risks restoring the exclusions along with the authority. The more plausible task is to build connections between publics rather than to merge them: institutions trusted across divides to verify claims, and habits of reporting that show their evidence so that readers who distrust the reporter can still examine the work. Such arrangements are less comforting than the image of a nation gathered around one screen, but they ask for something a plural society can actually provide. Nor need the connections be grand. A local paper that publishes the documents behind its reporting on a disputed planning decision, so that both sides can read them, does a small part of the work that the lament imagines only a national institution could do.

passage: Imagine a middle-income country that discovers large reserves of natural gas off its coast. Export earnings surge, foreign currency pours in, and the national currency rises in value. For a while the effects look wholly benign: imports become cheaper, the government collects more revenue, and wages climb as the gas sector and the services that cater to it compete for workers. Yet a decade later the country's manufacturers, who sell abroad against foreign rivals, may find themselves in serious trouble. A stronger currency makes their goods dearer in foreign markets, and the higher wages set by the booming sectors raise their costs at home. Factories close or move away, and the economy comes to rest ever more heavily on a single commodity. The pattern is common enough to have a name, Dutch disease, taken from the experience of the Netherlands after its large gas discoveries.

Some economists see nothing pathological in this. A country that finds itself rich in gas, they argue, should export gas and import the manufactures it once made, just as a country with fertile land should grow food. The movement of labour and capital out of factories is, on this account, the market reallocating resources to where they now earn most. To call it a disease is to mistake adjustment for illness.

The argument is coherent, but it assumes that the sectors lost can be regained whenever conditions change, and that assumption is doubtful. Manufacturing is not merely one way among others of earning foreign exchange. It is a place where workers acquire skills, where firms learn by doing, and where suppliers, engineers and managers accumulate knowledge that exists in no manual. Such capabilities take years to build and decay quickly once the firms that hold them have gone. Gas, meanwhile, is finite, and its price is notoriously volatile. When the price falls or the fields run down, the currency weakens and exporting becomes profitable again in principle, but the firms, skills and networks that would have taken advantage of the change no longer exist. The country finds that it cannot simply return to where it was.

The remedy, then, is not to leave the gas in the ground but to manage the boom so that it does not hollow out everything else. A government can save a large share of the windfall abroad, in a fund invested in foreign assets, which slows the rise of the currency and spreads the benefit across generations; it can spend at home at a pace the economy can absorb without bidding up wages across the board. Such measures are politically hard, because they ask citizens to forgo spending money they can see. But the alternative is to treat a temporary gift as permanent income, and to discover too late that the industries it displaced were not as replaceable as the theory assumed.

options.B: their most skilled engineers and managers are recruited to run the government's new fund invested abroad.

passage: Few school practices seem as commonsensical as grouping pupils by ability. A teacher facing a class whose members range from those who can barely read to those who devour novels must, it seems, either bore the strong or lose the weak, and sorting children into streams promises to spare her that dilemma. Each group can be taught at its own pace, with material pitched to its level; nobody is held back and nobody is left behind. The argument has the appeal of efficiency, and in a narrow sense it is often right.

The trouble lies in what a stream does after it has been formed. Placement usually happens early and rests on tests that measure, along with ability, a child's maturity, her familiarity with the kind of task being set and the amount of help she has had at home. Children who are young for their year are a familiar case: a few months' difference that would be invisible at fifteen can look like a difference of talent at seven. Once placed, however, pupils do not simply learn at different speeds. The lower streams are often given a thinner curriculum, less experienced teachers and quieter expectations, while the upper streams are prepared for examinations the others will never be entered for. The gap that the original test detected is thus widened by the arrangement that was supposed to respond to it, and the later results, which seem to confirm the placement, are partly its product.

Defenders of streaming reply that pupils can move between groups, and in principle they can. In practice movement is uncommon, and it is not difficult to see why. A child in a lower stream who has covered less material cannot readily join a group that has covered more, so even a genuine improvement in her understanding may never show up as a change of placement. Teachers, moreover, come to know their pupils as members of a particular set, and the label shapes how her work is read. The door is open, but the corridor behind it grows longer every term.

It would be a mistake to conclude that all grouping is harmful. Teaching a class of widely mixed attainment is genuinely demanding, and some arrangements avoid the worst effects of streaming: grouping pupils separately for particular subjects, regrouping them frequently and keeping the curriculum common, so that a move between groups remains a realistic possibility rather than a formal one. What distinguishes these arrangements from the rigid stream is not that they ignore differences in attainment but that they refuse to treat a single early measurement as a verdict.

passage: In a society whose members hold different and often incompatible views about the meaning of life and the sources of value, on what basis may some of them use the power of the state to make others comply with laws? One influential answer holds that coercive laws must be justifiable by reasons that all reasonable citizens could accept, whatever their wider convictions. A law defended solely by appeal to a doctrine that many of one's fellow citizens reject, whether that doctrine is religious or secular, treats them as subjects to be managed rather than as equals to be persuaded. The requirement to offer such shared, or public, reasons is usually called the ideal of public reason.

Critics have objected that the ideal asks too much of ordinary citizens. People do not keep their deepest convictions in a compartment separate from their political views; for many, their sense of what justice requires flows directly from a philosophical or religious outlook. To tell such citizens that they may vote, campaign and argue only on grounds detachable from that outlook is to ask them to enter public life as strangers to themselves. Worse, the demand seems to fall unevenly, since those whose convictions already happen to resemble the shared vocabulary are asked to give up nothing.

Much of this objection depends on reading the ideal as a rule about what citizens may say. It is more plausible to read it as a test that laws must pass. On this reading a citizen may give whatever reasons move her, in the street, in the press or in the voting booth, and the ideal is satisfied so long as the law that is eventually enacted can also be supported by reasons that do not depend on any one contested doctrine. The burden then falls most heavily on those who exercise official power, on legislators drafting statutes and judges explaining decisions, rather than on citizens in conversation with one another.

This reading does not remove every difficulty. If a citizen offers public reasons she does not herself find convincing, merely because she knows they are the only reasons that will count, her contribution begins to look less like persuasion and more like strategy. The ideal was meant to express respect for others as fellow reasoners, and insincere argument is a poor vehicle for respect. But this worry, though real, tells against a particular style of advocacy rather than against the test itself. A law can be justified in shared terms even if some of its supporters were moved by other considerations, just as a bridge can be sound though some of those who voted to build it understood nothing of engineering.

passage: Give a group of people an ordinary object, a coffee mug, say, or a pen, and then ask them how much they would accept to sell it; ask another group, who were not given the object, how much they would pay to acquire one. In experiments of this kind the sellers' prices have repeatedly been found to exceed the buyers' by a wide margin, even though the two groups were formed at random and there is no reason to think that the owners care more for mugs. Merely owning a thing, it seems, makes it more valuable to its owner. The finding has come to be known as the endowment effect, and it has become one of the best-known results in behavioural economics.

The standard interpretation explains it by loss aversion. People, on this view, evaluate outcomes not in absolute terms but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Once the mug is mine, giving it up registers as a loss, whereas acquiring it, for someone who does not own it, registers only as a gain, and since the loss weighs more heavily, the owner demands more in compensation than the non-owner will pay. The account is economical, and it connects the mug experiments with a wide range of other behaviour, from the reluctance of investors to sell shares that have fallen in value to the stubbornness with which people defend entitlements they have only recently acquired.

A rival interpretation treats the gap as, at least in part, an artefact of the way such experiments are conducted. Participants who have never sold anything in a laboratory may be unsure what is being asked, may suspect that the experimenter knows the object's true value, or may simply apply a rule from everyday life, never to sell for less than it would cost to replace the thing. When procedures are altered so that participants practise the bidding mechanism and understand that misstating their values cannot help them, some studies have found the gap to shrink considerably. Supporters of this view also point out that professional traders, who buy and sell as a matter of routine, appear to show much less of the effect in the goods they deal in.

Each interpretation captures something real, and the dispute is less sharp than it is sometimes made to appear. The traders' case is telling not because it refutes loss aversion but because it suggests where loss aversion applies. A dealer who holds a stock of mugs holds them in order to sell them; parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss. A person who has been given a mug to use is in a different position, because the mug has already become, in a small way, part of her possessions, and parting with it means giving something up rather than completing a transaction. On this reading, what matters is not ownership as such but the frame in which a thing is held, as something to use or as something to exchange.

That reading has consequences beyond the laboratory. It implies that the gap between buying and selling prices is not a fixed constant of human nature, to be entered into economic models as a permanent correction, but a variable that depends on how people come to think of what they have. Markets that encourage people to regard their possessions as stock, as resale platforms arguably do, may weaken the effect; arrangements that encourage people to regard what they hold as their own, as long trial periods for products arguably do, may strengthen it. Whether either tendency is desirable is a separate question. The point is that the endowment effect, properly understood, is less a fact about objects or owners than a fact about the relation between them.
